task: Prepare for and run a business-to-business negotiation with a partner from a different culture and reach a deal that holds.
condition: Given a supplier or buyer case with price, delivery and payment figures and a short profile of the other side's working style.
standard: The preparation sheet has correct limits and a deal zone, and the final deal lies inside the zone with reasons recorded.
who: Managers who buy, sell or partner across borders and need deals that survive after the handshake.

modules.title: The four parts of cultural intelligence
modules.intro: Cultural intelligence is the skill of working well with people whose habits differ from yours. It has four parts: drive, knowledge, strategy and action.
points: Drive: wish to learn
Knowledge: facts about the other culture
Strategy: planning and checking
Action: changing what you do
modules.example: A manager rates herself 1 to 7 on four parts: drive 6, knowledge 3, strategy 4, action 5. Average = (6+3+4+5)/4 = 4.5. The lowest is knowledge at 3, so she spends her first 4 prep hours reading about the partner's business customs rather than rehearsing her pitch.
modules.activity: Rate yourself on each of the four parts with one real example each, and choose the lowest part to improve.
modules.standard: Four ratings with four examples, a correct average, and one named improvement action.

modules.title: Reading direct and indirect messages
modules.intro: Some people say what they mean in words; others let the situation carry the meaning. Misreading this costs deals.
points: Direct style: the words carry the meaning
Indirect style: tone, pauses and setting carry it
Check meaning by asking neutral questions
modules.example: A supplier writes: 'This will be difficult to arrange in that time.' A direct reader hears 'maybe'. An indirect reader hears 'no'. Test: the supplier offers no new date. Count of signals for 'no': no date offered, hedged wording, copy to a senior person = 3 of 3. Reading: treat as no and ask 'What time would be easier?'.
modules.activity: Read five short messages and mark each as likely yes, maybe or no with the signals that support the mark.
modules.standard: At least four of five readings match the model answers and each has two signals named.

modules.title: Time, trust and relationship building
modules.intro: In some places trust comes first and a deal follows. In others the deal is the way to build trust. Plan time for both.
points: Estimate meetings needed to reach trust
Count the cost of relationship time
Fix the deal clock to match
modules.example: Home market: 3 meetings of 2 hours to a deal = 6 hours. Partner market: 9 meetings of 3 hours on average, 4 of them meals = 27 hours. Extra time = 27 - 6 = 21 hours. At a manager cost of 90 an hour that is 1,890. If the deal is worth 400,000 the cost is under 0.5%, so the relationship time is easily justified.
modules.activity: Estimate the hours to close a deal in two different markets and compare the cost with deal value.
modules.standard: Both time estimates are shown with working and the percentage cost is correct.

modules.title: Preparing limits and the deal zone
modules.intro: Before talking, know your walk-away point, your best alternative and the other side's likely limit. The overlap is the deal zone.
points: Reservation point: the worst deal you accept
Best alternative: what you do if no deal
Deal zone: where both sides could say yes
modules.example: A buyer will pay at most 120 a unit; the best alternative costs 115 after extra shipping, so the real limit is 115. The seller needs at least 95. The zone is 95 to 115, width 20. If the buyer's guess of the seller's limit is wrong and the seller needs 118, there is no zone, and the buyer must change the alternative or the specification.
modules.activity: Fill in a preparation sheet with both sides' limits, alternatives and the deal zone for a case you are given.
modules.standard: Both limits, both alternatives and the zone width are correct and the sheet names one assumption to test.

modules.title: Opening offers and the pattern of concessions
modules.intro: Where you start and how you move tells the other side what to expect. Cultures read concessions differently.
points: First offers anchor the talk
Concessions should shrink as you near your limit
Never concede without asking for something
modules.example: A seller wants a target price of 110 and a floor of 100. Opens at 130. Planned steps: 130, 120, 114, 110, 108. Gaps: 10, 6, 4, 2. Shrinking gaps signal the floor is near. Total moved = 130 - 108 = 22. In a market where haggling is a sign of respect, a first move of only 3 would seem rude.
modules.activity: Plan a five-step concession ladder for a case, with a trade requested at each step.
modules.standard: Steps shrink, none passes the limit and each step lists what is asked in return.

modules.title: Multi-issue trades
modules.intro: Most deals have more than price. Trading issues each side values differently can make both better off.
points: List issues and give each a value to each side
Trade what is cheap for you and dear to them
Check the total value, not each issue
modules.example: Value of fast delivery: 6 points to the buyer, 2 points of cost to the seller. Value of a 3-point price cut: 3 points to the buyer, 3 points of cost to the seller. Trade: the seller gives fast delivery and the buyer gives up the price cut. Buyer gets 6 and gives up 3, so gains 3. Seller spends 2 and saves 3, so gains 1. Both are ahead, and the pair gains 4 in total.
modules.activity: Rank four issues for each side in a case and propose two trades that leave both sides better off.
modules.standard: Two trades with the gain to each side shown in numbers and both gains above zero.

modules.title: Hierarchy and decision making
modules.intro: Who decides, and how, differs by culture. Some decide alone at the top; others agree in groups before anyone speaks.
points: Map the real decision path
Estimate days per level
Find the person who can say no
modules.example: Partner firm: 4 approval levels at 5 working days each = 20 days. Add a month-end freeze of 6 days. Expected decision = 26 working days. If your deadline is in 15 days, you are 11 days short. Option: ask for a pre-approval meeting with the second level, which could remove two levels and save 10 days.
modules.activity: Draw the decision path for a partner and calculate the expected time to decision against your deadline.
modules.standard: A path with levels, a correct total and one action that shortens it.

modules.title: Closing, writing the contract and keeping the bond
modules.intro: A contract is read differently in different places. Close the deal with clear terms and keep the relationship working afterwards.
points: Write clear measurable terms
Agree how disputes are raised
Plan a first-90-day review
modules.example: A contract for 2,000,000 over two years. Unclear delivery wording leads to a dispute costing an estimated 3% = 60,000 plus 4 weeks delay. Clear wording: 'delivered to the named port by the 15th of each month, 5% fine per week late'. A 90-day review meeting at day 90 catches issues before the first quarter payment of 250,000.
modules.activity: Write five measurable terms and a dispute step for a deal, then plan the 90-day review.
modules.standard: Five terms with number, date or test, one dispute step, and a dated review.

quiz.q: A manager rates drive 6, knowledge 3, strategy 4, action 5. What is her average and which part gets work first?
A supplier says 'This will be difficult' and offers no date. How might an indirect reader take it?
quiz.a: As a polite no, and the next step is to ask what time would be easier.

quiz.q: A deal takes 6 hours at home and 27 hours in the partner market. What is the extra cost at 90 an hour?
A buyer's stated limit is 120 but the alternative costs 115. What is the real limit?
quiz.a: 115, because paying more than the alternative makes no sense.

quiz.q: The buyer's real limit is 115 and the seller's floor is 95. How wide is the zone?
A seller steps 130, 120, 114, 110, 108. What are the gaps and what do they tell the buyer?
quiz.a: 10, 6, 4, 2; shrinking gaps signal the floor is near.

quiz.q: Why should every concession in a ladder be paired with an ask?
quiz.a: Giving without asking teaches the other side that pushing works and leaves value unused.

quiz.q: Delivery is worth 6 to the buyer and costs the seller 2. What is the net value of trading it?
quiz.a: Buyer gains 6, seller loses 2, so the pair gains 4 in total.

quiz.q: Four levels at 5 days each plus 6 freeze days against a 15-day deadline. By how many days do you miss it?
A 3% dispute cost on a 2,000,000 contract is how much?

ladder.title: L1 Basic: Why culture changes a deal
ladder.slide: Two honest people can read the same sentence differently. A deal fails when each side assumes the other reads it their way.
ladder.notes: Say: tell a short story of a misread yes. Check: ask learners for one case. Mistake: blaming bad faith.

ladder.title: L2 The four parts of cultural intelligence
ladder.slide: Drive, knowledge, strategy and action. We rate ourselves and pick the lowest part.
ladder.notes: Say: all four are skills, not talent. Check: each learner names their lowest. Mistake: rating only drive.

ladder.title: L3 Reading messages
ladder.slide: Direct words or indirect signals. Count the signals before you decide what was meant.
ladder.notes: Say: use the supplier example. Check: mark three messages. Mistake: reading one signal alone.

ladder.title: L4 Time and trust
ladder.slide: Relationship time is a cost with a return. Estimate hours and compare with deal value.
ladder.notes: Say: show the 21-hour gap. Check: compute percentage. Mistake: treating meals as waste.

ladder.title: L5 Limits and the deal zone
ladder.slide: Know your limit, your alternative and theirs. The overlap is the zone.
ladder.notes: Say: show a zone and a no-zone case. Check: learners find the zone. Mistake: using the stated limit instead of the alternative.

ladder.title: L6 Concessions and trades
ladder.slide: Move in shrinking steps and always ask for something. Trade what is cheap to you and dear to them.
ladder.notes: Say: draw the ladder. Check: no step passes the limit. Mistake: matching their moves exactly.

ladder.title: L7 Deciding, closing and keeping the bond
ladder.slide: Map who really decides, write measurable terms and review at 90 days.
ladder.notes: Say: ask who can say no. Check: does every term have a number or date? Mistake: closing with vague words.

rubric.not_yet: Limits or deal zone missing or wrong.
rubric.meets: Limits, alternatives and zone are correct.
rubric.exceeds: Also tests the main assumption and plans a response if it is wrong.

rubric.not_yet: Reads behaviour by home-culture rules only.
rubric.meets: Names signals and offers two readings before acting.
rubric.exceeds: Checks the reading with a neutral question and adjusts the plan.

rubric.not_yet: Concessions with no asks, or past the limit.
rubric.meets: Shrinking steps with trades, inside the zone.
rubric.exceeds: Finds a trade that leaves both sides better off and shows the numbers.

rubric.meets: Clear terms, dispute step and review date.
rubric.exceeds: Terms anticipate a likely problem and include a fair fix.

jobs.what: Wins and renews deals with customers in other countries.
Buys from suppliers abroad and keeps prices and delivery on target.
Builds and manages joint ventures and distribution agreements.
Writes and reviews cross-border contract terms and dispute steps.
